contexts.name: Booking
contexts.businessModelSays: no row — Booking is absent from the capability table
contexts.classificationNote: The business model never classified Booking, so "core" is unbacked. This is the context the map calls "where the money is committed".

invariants.text: A booking may only be confirmed once its capacity has been reserved
…but the capacity rule itself lives in Consolidation, and Booking reads it synchronously before reserving

language.definition: A customer's committed request to move a consignment on a given departure
The goods a customer hands over as one unit
language.note: Invoicing defines the same word as "a billable line on an invoice"

gaps.text: "Consignment" means physical goods here and a billable line in Invoicing — hotspot #2, unresolved.
Writes ConsignmentLine, which the context map declares a Shared Kernel with Consolidation — but the two sides already model different attributes.

contexts.name: Consolidation
contexts.businessModelSays: revenue-generator · custom-built · differentiation: YES — "the premium customers pay for; a new entrant would need both the depot network and the planning know-how"
contexts.classificationNote: Classified supporting ("back-office load planning"), but it is the only capability the business model marks as differentiating and revenue-generating.

invariants.text: A container's committed volume must never exceed its capacity
invariants.note: Owned here, checked from Booking, enforced nowhere agreed — hotspot #1

language.definition: The set of consignments committed to one physical container on one departure
Committed volume divided by container capacity

gaps.text: The differentiating know-how is not in the model: "load planning still happens partly on a whiteboard in the Gothenburg depot", four senior planners resolve infeasible stacks by hand.
The short-term goal is 71% -> 80% container fill. Nothing in the model represents the optimiser, the stacking rules, or the fill target.
Guaranteed Consolidation (+18% premium, promises a departure slot) is a revenue stream with no aggregate, no invariant and no event.

contexts.name: Routing
contexts.businessModelSays: cost-reduction · product · differentiation: no — "the partner network is the asset, not the routing step"
contexts.classificationNote: Context map and business model agree.
contexts.aggregatesRationale: Routing receives BookingConfirmed and hands the shipment to the partner carrier selected by the standing contract for that lane. It owns no rule of its own.

gaps.text: Hotspot #3: nobody knows who is responsible when a partner carrier refuses a sealed container. No event, no owner, no aggregate covers the refusal.

contexts.name: Customs
contexts.businessModelSays: compliance-enforcer · product · differentiation: no — "required, and two vendors already do it well"
contexts.classificationNote: Classified core ("regulated, and mistakes are expensive"). The business model says no differentiation, and the model note says two commercial platforms already cover all nine ports — "we integrate with neither". Regulated is not the same as core.

invariants.text: A shipment cannot be handed to a carrier before its declaration is submitted

gaps.text: No ubiquitous-language terms — for the context the map calls regulated and expensive to get wrong.
12 tables, 96 attributes, densest entity 34 attributes — modelled as one entity with 4.
No rejection path. DeclarationSubmitted and DeclarationCleared exist; nothing models a declaration being refused.
"Two commercial customs platforms cover all nine ports; we integrate with neither" — build-vs-buy is open and unowned.

contexts.name: Invoicing
contexts.businessModelSays: compliance-enforcer · commodity · differentiation: NO — "nobody has ever chosen us because of our invoices"
contexts.classificationNote: Context map calls it core because it is "the largest and most business-critical system we run". Largest is not core. The business model rates it commodity with zero differentiation.

invariants.text: An invoice line must reference a cleared declaration

language.definition: A billable line on an invoice
language.note: Booking defines the same word as physical goods

language.definition: Any fee added to the forwarding rate

gaps.text: 4 of 5 aggregates are a name and nothing else — no entities, no attributes, no events.
CreditNote, DunningCase and PaymentAllocation exist as aggregates but emit no events. Credit, dunning and payment are invisible in the flow.
Densest entity: 128 attributes. That is not an entity, that is a table.
51% of all modelled attributes in the company sit in the context the business explicitly calls a commodity.

conflicts.title: The core/supporting map contradicts the business model
conflicts.detail: Consolidation is the only capability the business model marks as differentiating and revenue-generating, and the context map files it as supporting. Invoicing and Customs are both filed core while the business model rates them commodity and product with no differentiation. Sub-domain type drives where the good engineers go — right now it points them at the invoice system.

conflicts.title: Nobody owns the capacity invariant
conflicts.detail: "A container's committed volume must never exceed its capacity" belongs to Consolidation's ContainerLoad. Booking enforces its own rule by reading remaining capacity synchronously and then reserving. Read-then-act across an aggregate boundary has no serialisation — which is exactly the March incident: two shipments committed to the same slot, and nobody agrees where the check should have happened.

conflicts.title: "Consignment" means two different things
conflicts.detail: Booking: the goods a customer hands over as one unit. Invoicing: a billable line on an invoice. Finance and operations have been using the word past each other (hotspot #2) and both definitions are written into the model as if settled.

conflicts.title: The Shared Kernel has already diverged
conflicts.detail: ConsignmentLine is declared a Shared Kernel written by both Booking and Consolidation. Booking models lineId, volumeM3, weightKg, hazardClass. Consolidation models lineId, volumeM3, stackable. Two writers, two shapes, no agreed contract.

conflicts.title: Modelling effort is inverted against differentiation
conflicts.detail: Invoicing: 34 tables, 311 attributes, densest entity 128 attributes, for a capability the commercial director describes as "nobody has ever chosen us because of our invoices". Consolidation: 5 tables, 41 attributes, and the actual planning still runs on a whiteboard in Gothenburg.

unknowns.text: No customer took part in either session. Every "what customers value" row is the commercial director speaking for them, marked proxy.
Cost structure per shipment — nobody in the room owns the P&L.
Whether customers would pay for guaranteed departure windows as a separate product — no customer has been asked.
Who is responsible when a partner carrier refuses a sealed container.
What Tariff Data is. It has an arrow on the context map and nothing else.
Every one of the 10 docs is status: draft with owner: TBD. The classification table "has not been revisited since the first modelling session in March".

decisions.ask: Re-classify Consolidation as core, and Invoicing + Customs as supporting/generic — or write down why the map is right and the business model is wrong.
Name the place the capacity invariant is enforced. One context, one transaction.
Rename one of the two Consignments. Suggested: Invoicing's becomes BillableLine.
Split ConsignmentLine per context, or pin the shared attribute set and give it one owner.
Confirm CustomerNotified with someone who knows, or delete it from the timeline.
Put a name against each of the 7 contexts. Owner TBD x10 is why none of the above got resolved since March.
Book a session with an actual customer before the next modelling round.
